title: Questions to Ask When Replacing an HVAC System
h1: What Questions Should You Ask When Replacing an HVAC System?
description: The questions to ask before replacing your HVAC system: sizing, ducts, efficiency, permits, warranties, refrigerant and what the quote should include.
quick_answer: Ask how the contractor will size the system, whether they'll inspect and test your ducts, what efficiency options fit your home, whether the job includes a permit, what refrigerant the new system uses, what the manufacturer and labor warranties cover, and exactly what's included in the quote. Clear answers to those questions separate a careful install from a quick swap.
body:
How will you size the new system?

This is the first question to ask, and the answer tells you a lot. A good contractor calculates your home's heating and cooling needs based on square footage, insulation, windows, which way the house faces, ceiling heights and duct location. That's usually called a load calculation.

A contractor who looks at your old unit and quotes the same size is guessing. The old system may have been oversized from the start, or your home may have changed since then with new windows, added insulation or a room addition. An oversized system short-cycles, leaves humidity behind and wears out faster. An undersized one runs nonstop on hot inland afternoons and still can't keep up.

What will you do about my ductwork?

New equipment connected to leaky, crushed or undersized ducts won't perform the way it should. Ask:

  • Will you inspect the ducts in the attic, garage or crawl space?
  • Will you test for duct leakage? California's energy code often requires duct testing when HVAC equipment is replaced, and the permit inspection checks for it.
  • Do any sections need sealing, repair or replacement?
  • Is the return side large enough for the new system's airflow?

In many San Diego and Orange County homes, the ducts are as old as the equipment and run through a hot attic. Replacing them at the same time is often worth considering.

What type of system makes sense for my home?

Ask the contractor to explain the options, not just quote one box. Common choices include:

  • Furnace and AC: the classic split system, with gas heat and electric cooling.
  • Heat pump: all-electric heating and cooling, a good fit for our mild winters.
  • Dual fuel: a heat pump paired with a gas furnace for backup on cold inland nights.
  • Ductless mini-splits: for additions, garages converted to living space or homes without ducts.

Also ask about single-stage versus two-stage or variable-speed equipment. Variable-speed systems run longer at lower output, which tends to mean steadier temperatures, better humidity control and quieter operation.

What efficiency rating should I choose?

Higher efficiency means lower operating costs but a higher upfront price. Ask the contractor to explain the ratings for the systems they're proposing (SEER2 for cooling, HSPF2 for heat pump heating, AFUE for gas furnaces) and how much you'd realistically use the system. A home near the coast that rarely runs AC has different priorities than an inland home that cools all summer.

Ask whether any utility rebates or manufacturer promotions apply. Programs change, so a current contractor should know what's available.

What does the quote include?

Quotes can look similar and be very different. Get these details in writing:

  1. Exact equipment brand, model numbers and efficiency ratings
  2. Permit and inspection
  3. Removal and disposal of old equipment, including proper refrigerant recovery
  4. New refrigerant lines or flushing of existing lines
  5. Duct work, sealing or replacement
  6. Thermostat
  7. Electrical work, pad, drain line and any needed platform or venting changes
  8. Equipment registration for the manufacturer warranty

What should happen on installation day?

Ask who will do the install and how long it will take. A careful installer protects floors and the work area, pulls a vacuum on the refrigerant lines before releasing refrigerant, checks the charge and airflow once the system runs, and confirms the condensate drain is working. Ask whether the technician will show you how to use the thermostat and change the filter before they leave.

If the equipment sits in an attic, ask how they'll get it up there and whether any platform, walkway or attic access work is included.

What about warranties, refrigerant and licensing?

Ask what the manufacturer warranty covers, how long it lasts, and whether registration is required. Ask separately about the contractor's labor warranty, since parts coverage doesn't pay for the labor to install them.

Ask which refrigerant the new system uses. Newer systems use different refrigerants than older ones, and it's worth knowing what you're getting. Finally, confirm the contractor holds an active license with the Contractors State License Board. Sky Clean Air operates under California Contractor License #1036543.

If you're weighing a replacement, our HVAC installation team can run the numbers for your home and walk you through options with a free estimate. Check current specials as well.
faqs: Should I repair or replace my HVAC system?

Consider replacing when the system is older and needs a major repair, when repairs are becoming frequent, when it can't keep the house comfortable, or when a cracked heat exchanger or failed compressor shows up. A technician can give you repair and replacement options so you can compare them side by side.
How long does an HVAC replacement take?

A straightforward replacement of a furnace and AC is often done in a day or two. Jobs that include new ductwork, a change in system type, added electrical work or relocating equipment take longer. The permit inspection is scheduled separately after installation.
Do I need a permit to replace my HVAC system?

In California, HVAC replacements generally require a permit, and the inspection checks the installation and, in many cases, duct leakage testing. Your contractor should pull the permit. Ask about it before signing.
Should I replace my ducts at the same time?

If your ducts are old, leaky, crushed or undersized, replacing them with the equipment is often the best time to do it. A new system on bad ducts won't deliver its rated performance. Ask your contractor to inspect and test the ducts before deciding.
